newsitem.title: BOSNIA: Kinkel says clock ticking for war crimes suspects.
newsitem.headline: Kinkel says clock ticking for war crimes suspects.

text.p: German Foreign Minister Klaus Kinkel hinted on Friday that the international community would not tolerate the presence of indicted war criminals in Bosnia indefinitely.
He noted during a visit to Sarajevo that the former warring factions had promised under a peace agreement to hand over suspects named by the U.N. war crimes tribunal in The Hague.
"Unfortunately this has not happened yet," Kinkel told a news conference.

Asked about the possibility of more NATO raids against suspects wanted by the tribunal, Kinkel said: "There were some measures already taken and first we have to see the conflicting parties fulfill what they have promised.
"Otherwise suspected war criminals will have to know that the clock is ticking."
Kinkel declined to elaborate but his comments reinforced a pledge delivered by NATO Secretary-General Javier Solana on Thursday.
Solana said in Washington that all war crimes suspects would be extradited by the time the international community left Bosnia-Herzegovina.
He did not specify whether he was referring to a June 1998 deadline when the NATO-led peace force is scheduled to withdraw.
Kinkel was visiting Bosnia two weeks after British soldiers swooped on two Serb war crimes suspects. One was extradited to The Hague and the other shot dead after he resisted arrest.
The NATO raid has raised expectations of more arrests, possibly targeting former Bosnian Serb president Radovan Karadzic, who still wields power behind the scenes in Serb territory.
Kinkel said delivery of economic aid would be linked to the war criminals issue and compliance with the Dayton peace agreement.

The German foreign minister was accompanied by Dietmar Schlee, newly-appointed German commissioner for refugees, who is supposed to oversee the return of Bosnians who fled to Germany during the Yugoslav conflict.
Germany accepted some 300,000 Bosnian refugees during the war, more than any other European country, but authorities are are now anxious for them to move back.
